title: Growth–defence trade-off defines a diffusion limit. A commentary on ‘Boundary-line trade-off in bryophytes between UV photoprotection and photosynthetic capacity, but not desiccation tolerance’
content: Bryophytes ‘buy’ biochemical protection from UV radiation by investment in cell-wall compounds such as biflavonoids, and the ‘bill’ comes due in a reduced CO2 supply (Perera Castro et al., 2025; this issue). For CO2 to enter the chloroplast, it must first pass through the cell wall. It is known from work with tracheophytes that thicker or phenolic-rich walls lower the conductance to CO2. Bryophytes, being already constrained by relatively thick walls, appear to reach the same diffusional ceiling (Roig-Oliver et al., 2020; Flexas et al., 2021). This is because thicker walls increase diffusion path length with higher phenolic loading, lowering effective porosity; together these factors reduce internal CO2 conductance (Fig. 1A). The absence of leaves with stomata in bryophytes amplifies the role of the cell wall as the primary interface controlling gas exchange. However, the broad relationships between UV-absorbing compounds and photosynthesis need clarification. To complicate matters, photochemistry, measured by chlorophyll fluorescence, can be active while assimilation is limited by CO2 supply, making the detection of CO2 diffusion limitations difficult.
